Asked about Trump's comment a day earlier that Kim possessed 57 "very powerful nuclear weapons", Ahn said, "the numbers appear somewhat different". Trump made the remark at the White House on Wednesday while discussing North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his plans to meet him later this year. South Korea has traditionally avoided publicly disclosing detailed estimates of North Korea's nuclear stockpile and does not officially recognise Pyongyang as a nuclear weapons state under its long-standing policy supporting denuclearisation. Ahn reiterated that position when asked whether the government acknowledged North Korea as a nuclear-armed state. "We cannot officially acknowledge that," he said. He also declined to comment on whether Trump's reference to 57 warheads amounted to US recognition of North Korea's nuclear status, saying it would not be appropriate for South Korea's defence minister to comment on the US president's remarks. Ahn said South Korea would continue to rely on the US nuclear umbrella, in line with Seoul's longstanding non-nuclear policy. "We cannot develop nuclear weapons. Nor should we accept the deployment of US tactical nuclear weapons," Ahn said. The comments came as Trump seeks to revive engagement with Kim after ordering a scale-back of joint US-South Korean military drills , which he described as "hostile" to North Korea. North Korea responded coolly to the move. Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of the North Korean leader, said the reduced exercises remained provocative and aggressive despite their shortened duration. She dismissed any suggestion that Pyongyang would view the move as a meaningful goodwill gesture and said she was unaware of any recent contacts between Trump and Kim, although she described the personal relationship between the leaders as "excellent." Trump said at the White House on Wednesday that he expected to meet Kim later this year , potentially reviving diplomacy that stalled after a series of unprecedented summits in 2018 and 2019 collapsed over disagreements on sanctions relief and North Korea's nuclear weapons programme.

Related:

US-South Korea drills cut short after Trump criticism

Source: Reuters/rk

Aug 19 (Reuters) - Indian fintech startup Navi said on Wednesday it will raise $100 million from Dutch technology investor Prosus NV in its first institutional funding round, a deal that comes ahead of a planned initial public offering, a source familiar with the matter said. Reuters could not determine the valuation at which Prosus made the investment. The investment values Navi at about $1.3 billion, the Economic Times reported on Wednesday, citing a person with direct knowledge of the matter.

Navi is seeking a valuation of about $2 billion in the IPO, the source said, declining to be named because the information is confidential. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its IPO plans or valuation. Navi was founded in 2018 by Sachin Bansal, a co-founder of Walmart-backed Indian e-commerce firm Flipkart. The company offers digital payments, lending, mutual funds and insurance through a digital platform. The investment is subject to regulatory approvals, including from the Competition Commission of India, Navi said in a statement. (Reporting by Ira Dugal in Mumbai and Urvi Dugar and Abinaya V in Bengaluru; Editing by Tasim Zahid)

item.title: China’s July Coal Output Falls to Pandemic-Era Levels in Wake of Deadly Accident
item.description: By Colleen Howe China’s coal output in July fell back to pandemic-era levels, statistics bureau data showed on Monday, as stepped-up safety oversight after a deadly mining accident continued to weigh on mining operations. Coal output in China, the world’s largest producer, fell 10.1% to 343.21 …
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded:
By Colleen Howe

China’s coal output in July fell back to pandemic-era levels, statistics bureau data showed on Monday, as stepped-up safety oversight after a deadly mining accident continued to weigh on mining operations.

Coal output in China, the world’s largest producer, fell 10.1% to 343.21 million metric tons in July from a year earlier, the National Bureau of Statistics said.

That was the lowest standalone monthly output figure reported since September 2021. That excludes output for the months of January and February, which are reported as a combined figure to smooth out the effects of the Lunar New Year holiday, which falls in either month and also affects production.

“This round of production declines was not caused by a weakening in demand, but rather stemmed from the continuous tightening of domestic coal mine safety regulations,” analysts at Galaxy Futures said in a note.

In May, 82 people were killed in a gas explosion at the Liushenyu mine in Shanxi province, the deadliest mining accident in 17 years, forcing many mines in the coal-rich province to close for inspections.

An initial probe into the incident found that the mine was using hidden tunnels and fake doors to shield some areas of the mine from regulatory oversight, state media reported.

“Many mines have voluntarily reduced their production loads after resuming operations, with significant reductions in Shanxi province in particular,” the Galaxy Futures analysts said.

The analysts forecast a 7%-9% year-on-year drop in August coal production and a 3%-5% decline for the full year, as tighter scrutiny forces mines to curb their previously undisclosed production.

Output for January-July reached 2.7 billion metric tons, down 2.9% compared with the same period last year, the statistics bureau data showed.

(Reporting by Colleen Howe; Editing by Sonali Paul and Emelia Sithole-Matarise)

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded:
China’s state iron ore buyer reached an agreement with Anglo American in April over an annual supply contract for the key steelmaking ingredient, three sources with knowledge of the matter said on Friday.

China Mineral Resources Group (CMRG), established in 2022 to assert more pricing power in the iron ore market where China is the dominant buyer, has stepped up efforts to win better terms for Chinese steelmakers grappling with dwindling demand and shrinking margins.

Bloomberg reported the news earlier on Friday.

Under the agreement, which had not previously been reported, CMRG became the exclusive sales agent in China for some iron ore from Anglo American’s Kumba unit in South Africa starting from April, the sources said.

Two of them said the deal was for around 10 million metric tons, to be supplied to CMRG’s member steel mills.

The contract will last through March 2027, one of them said. The sources all declined to be named as they were not authorized to speak with media.

Kumba’s  iron ore sales  stood at 18.6 million tons in the first half of the year, with sales to China accounting for 54% of that.

Ebrahim Dadoo, Anglo American’s global head of sales and trading, said on an earnings call on July 28 that not all of that 54% went to CMRG, without providing further details.

CMRG did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Anglo American declined to comment.

In April, CMRG  reached  a supply agreement with BHP Group, ending a months-long dispute during which Chinese steelmakers and traders were barred from buying some BHP iron ore brands.
